939.title: Azusa Street (1906)
939.hook: a Black preacher, William Seymour, leads a revival in a plain Los Angeles mission building where races worship together
939.howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians often worship with spontaneous singing, raised hands, prayer for healing and prayer in tongues, and some churches remember Azusa Street as one of their beginnings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles de Foucauld, the officer turned hermit who wanted to be a universal brother in the Sahara.

Sawdust on the floor. Planks laid across boxes for benches. A shabby building on a side street in Los Angeles, once used for storage and, by some accounts, as a stable. The preacher at the front is a Black man named William Seymour, the son of formerly enslaved parents, blind in one eye. Sometimes he prays with his head inside an empty wooden crate. And the room is packed: Black washerwomen, white laborers, Mexican families, newcomers from all over, kneeling side by side, in a country where race usually kept people apart. Newspapers mocked it. People kept coming.
screen: `A PREACHER WITH HIS HEAD IN A CRATE.`

segments.voice: The people at Azusa Street said they were living through the Book of Acts again. On the day of Pentecost, Acts says, the first followers of Jesus were gathered in one place, and in the King James Bible: "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." At Azusa Street people prayed aloud in tongues, sang without hymnbooks, wept, shouted, fell quiet, and prayed for the sick, day after day. Pentecostal churches tell it as one of their beginnings, and so do some charismatic Christians in other churches. Here Christians differ, so plainly: Pentecostals hold that the gifts in Acts, tongues and healing among them, are for today. Some other Christians believe those gifts belonged mainly to the apostles' time, and worship in quieter ways. Both read the same Bible. Now the line. A white participant, Frank Bartleman, wrote afterward that at Azusa Street the color line was washed away in the blood, meaning the blood of Christ. Where race divided churches and much else, a Black preacher led, and people of every color prayed for each other. Paul had written it long before: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." The unity didn't last everywhere. In the years after, some churches that grew out of the revival split along the same color line again. That's part of the story. So is the room where, for a while, it was washed away.

Recall the last place you prayed, sang or sat in silence with others, and see who was in the room: who looked like you, and who didn't. Don't judge it; just see it. Then think of one place nearby where people unlike you gather, and if you pray, pray for that room, or simply hold it in mind.
Azusa Street. A side street in Los Angeles where a Black preacher led a revival, and people of every color knelt together.
Your line: the color line washed away. For a while, in one room, it was. That's day nine hundred thirty-nine.

940.title: Pandita Ramabai
940.hook: an Indian scholar and reformer who founded a home for widows and translated the Bible into Marathi
940.howItsDone: The community Ramabai founded near Pune still cares for women and children, and Marathi-speaking Christians remember her as a translator of their Bible.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Azusa Street, where a Black preacher led and people of every color knelt together: the color line washed away.

A young woman stands before a hall of learned men in Calcutta, recites long passages of Sanskrit verse from memory, and answers their questions. They're so impressed they give her titles of honor, and one sticks to her name for life: Pandita, a learned woman. Her father had taught her Sanskrit himself, a gift not every girl of her time was given. She has walked across much of India with her family. Soon she'll be married, then widowed, with a baby daughter in her arms. What she builds next will be a door for women with nowhere else to go.

In the India Ramabai grew up in, a widow's life could be very hard. Some were only girls when their husbands died. Custom in some families could mean a shaved head, plain clothes, no remarriage, no schooling, and a life at the back of the house. Hindu reformers of her day were working to change this too. Ramabai knew it from the inside. After her husband's death she traveled to England, and there, among Anglican sisters, she was baptized. She kept asking questions the whole way and didn't take everything on trust. In America she lectured and raised support. Then she came home and did something practical: she opened a home for widows, where they could live safely and, just as important, learn. Later she built a larger community on farmland outside Pune and called it Mukti, a word for freedom or deliverance. Women and girls who had been turned away found beds, classrooms, work and dignity there. Her reason was in the Bible she now read. The Letter of James puts it bluntly, in the King James Bible: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." Not only feel for them. Visit them. Ramabai gave them a home. And in her later years she translated the whole Bible into Marathi, her people's everyday language, working from the Hebrew and Greek herself. The scholar who once recited Sanskrit to learned men made sure the women of her region could read scripture in the words they spoke at home.

Think of a woman who taught you something: a teacher, a grandmother, a coworker who showed you the ropes. Then think of the women and girls still kept from school today, by money, by custom or by war. If you pray, pray for one of them; if not, hold her in mind, with thanks for the woman who taught you.
Pandita Ramabai. A Sanskrit scholar from India who became a Christian, opened a home for widows, and translated the Bible into Marathi.
Your line: a home for widows. Not only feeling for them, but making room. Day nine hundred forty, done.

941.title: Sadhu Sundar Singh
941.hook: a Sikh-born Indian who became a wandering Christian holy man in saffron robes
941.howItsDone: Christians in South Asia worship in many styles, and some use Indian forms such as sitting on the floor, bhajan-style songs and saffron dress for those who live as wandering preachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pandita Ramabai, the Sanskrit scholar who gave widows a home and the Bible in Marathi.

A traveler on a hot day in India collapses on a railway platform. Someone runs for water and comes back with it in a cup that belongs to the railway. The man on the ground, half fainting, refuses to drink. Not because he isn't thirsty. Because of the cup. Then someone brings the same water in his own brass vessel, and he drinks it gladly. A wandering holy man in a saffron robe told that story, to say something about the gospel and India.

Sundar Singh grew up in a Sikh family in the Punjab. His mother, by his own telling, took him to hear holy men and read sacred writings, and he loved her deeply. When she died he was young, and in his grief he grew angry at everything, including the Christian missionaries' book, which by his own account he tore and burned. Then, his story goes, he prayed through a night asking God to show himself, and before dawn he saw Jesus. He became a Christian. His family could not accept it, and he left home. India already had a figure everyone recognized: the sadhu, the wandering holy man with no possessions, walking village to village in a saffron robe. Sundar Singh put on that robe. He walked barefoot, slept where he was offered a place, and told stories about Jesus in the languages of the villages. He went over the mountain passes into Tibet to preach, and from his last journey there he never came back. Nobody knows what happened to him. The railway story answered a question: why does the gospel sometimes sound foreign in India? Because, he said, it had been handed over in a European cup. The water was what people needed. Jesus told a woman at a well, in the King James Bible: "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst." That water, Sundar Singh said, can come in an Indian cup. Christians still disagree about how much of a culture the gospel should wear. His answer was a saffron robe and bare feet.

Ask yourself what shape stillness takes in your life: a song from your grandmother's kitchen, a language you speak only at home, sitting cross-legged, kneeling or walking. For these two minutes, use your own cup. If you pray, pray in the words and posture that feel like home; if you don't, sit the way your body knows best.
sadhu. The Indian wandering holy man, the robe and life Sundar Singh took on after he left his Sikh family to follow Jesus.
Your line: water in an Indian cup. The same water, in a cup that fits. See you tomorrow.

942.title: The prophet Harris
942.hook: a Liberian evangelist walks West Africa in a white robe, and tradition says crowds are baptized
942.howItsDone: Members of the Harrist Church in Côte d'Ivoire, and some Methodists in the region, remember William Wadé Harris as the preacher who first brought the gospel to their villages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sadhu Sundar Singh and his railway story: the gospel's water in an Indian cup.

A prison cell in Liberia. The man inside is a schoolteacher and church worker named William Wadé Harris, locked up for his part in a political protest. By his own account, an angel comes to him there in a vision and tells him to put away his European clothes, dress simply, and go out as a preacher. When he walks out of prison, he does exactly that: a long white gown, a tall staff with a cross on top, a Bible, and a gourd rattle to call people together. No mission board sent him. No salary is waiting. He sets off along the coast on foot.
screen: `A WHITE GOWN, A CROSS-STAFF, A BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Harris walked east, out of Liberia, along the coast of what is now Côte d'Ivoire and into what is now Ghana. Village to village, on foot. He preached in simple words, prayed for the sick, and baptized people who wanted to follow Jesus. Tradition says the crowds grew so large that colonial officials grew nervous and finally sent him back home. His time on the road was short. Then the surprise. Harris didn't build his own organization. He told the new believers to build simple prayer houses, keep Sunday, and wait: teachers with the Bible would come, and they should listen. Then he walked on. Years later, missionaries arriving in some of those villages found congregations already gathered, keeping Sunday, singing, and waiting for someone to teach them. Some joined the Methodist church. Others kept his name and founded the Harrist Church, which continues today. Christians describe him differently: an evangelist, a prophet, a forerunner of the independent African churches. He called himself a prophet. Isaiah has a line for people like him, in the King James Bible: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace." It praises the feet. Not the voice, not the robe. Harris preached with his walking. Every village heard him because he had walked there.

If you can, stand and walk slowly, in a room or outside, feeling each step land, heel then toe; if you can't walk, let each breath be a step. With each step, name one person or place you'll pass today: the office, the bus driver, a neighbor's door. If you pray, carry each one to God as you go; if not, simply carry them with you.
Harris. A Liberian preacher who walked the West African coast in a white gown with a cross-staff, telling new believers to wait for teachers with the Bible.
Your line: the walking prophet. He let his feet do the preaching. Day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: Simon Kimbangu
943.hook: a Congolese healer spends the rest of his life in prison, and a church grows from it
943.howItsDone: Kimbanguists gather at Nkamba, which they call a holy place, to pray and sing, and they honor Simon Kimbangu as a prophet who suffered for the gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prophet Harris, who walked the West African coast and told new believers to wait for teachers.

Nkamba is a village in the hills of the lower Congo. One day, the story goes, a Baptist catechist named Simon Kimbangu lays his hands on a sick woman and prays, and she gets up. Word spreads. Soon the paths into the village are worn down by people carrying the sick on their backs and on stretchers. Markets empty. Some workers walk off their jobs to go and hear him. The Belgian colonial officials who run the Congo don't like any of it. A crowd that big, following a Congolese man, looks to them like trouble.

Kimbangu's public ministry was short. He preached from the Bible, prayed for the sick, told people to turn from violence and put away old objects of spiritual power, and called them to follow Jesus. The authorities ordered his arrest. For a while he stayed out of reach. Then, tradition says, he gave himself up and told his followers not to fight for him. It echoes that night in Gethsemane, when Jesus said to the disciple who drew a sword, in the King James Bible: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." A colonial court sentenced him to death. The sentence was changed to life in prison, and he was taken to a prison at the other end of the country. He never came home. He died there. Here's the strange part. The man was locked away, his followers watched, some exiled to distant parts of the colony, and the movement didn't vanish. It spread. Exiled families carried his teaching wherever they were sent. Out of it grew a church, the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth through the Prophet Simon Kimbangu, which Kimbanguists say grew from his suffering. They honor him as God's prophet. Other churches describe him in their own ways, and some differ with Kimbanguists about his place. Hebrews asks Christians to remember people in prison, in the King James words, "as bound with them". For Kimbanguists, the prison isn't where the story ended. It's where the church began.

Congo is a huge country of rivers, forests and cities, of families, churches, mosques and markets, and it has known a great deal of suffering. Picture one family there this evening: a meal cooking, children at homework, someone worried about tomorrow. If you pray, ask peace for that family; if you don't, let your attention rest on them, the way you'd hold a friend's name.
Simon Kimbangu. A Congolese catechist and healer who gave himself up, died in a colonial prison, and whose followers built a church.
Your line: a church from a prison. What was shut away kept growing. Until tomorrow.

944.title: The new martyrs of Russia
944.hook: after the Russian Revolution, priests, nuns and lay people are killed or sent to camps
944.howItsDone: The Russian Orthodox Church keeps a feast of the new martyrs and confessors of Russia, with icons that gather many of them together, and parishes pray for those who suffer for their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simon Kimbangu, who gave himself up, died in a colonial prison, and left a church growing behind him.

Before the revolution, she was a princess. Elizabeth, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, married into the Russian royal family. When a bomb killed her husband, she went to the prison, visited the man who had thrown it, and told him she forgave him. Then she gave away her jewels, put on a plain religious habit, and opened a convent in Moscow to nurse the poor. After the revolution, she was arrested. Tradition says that when her captors threw her and others down a mine shaft, people heard them singing hymns from below.

After the Russian Revolution, the new Soviet state set out to push religion out of public life. Churches were closed, looted, turned into warehouses or blown up. Bishops, priests, monks and nuns were shot or sent to labor camps in the far north and east. So were ordinary parishioners: a church warden, a choir singer, a grandmother who hid icons. On the island of Solovki, an old monastery became a prison camp. The Orthodox Church calls these people the new martyrs and confessors of Russia. A martyr dies for the faith; a confessor suffers for it and lives. Now the word inside the word. Before Jesus rises into heaven, he tells his followers, in the King James Bible: "ye shall be witnesses unto me." Later the Greek word behind witness is put into English another way, in Revelation: "Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you." Witness and martyr, one word. A martyr is first a witness. What did these witnesses do? Accounts from the camps describe priests hearing confessions in whispers during work, Easter hymns sung under the breath in a barracks, bread saved to share with someone weaker. Faithfulness in small hidden ways, where it could cost everything. Revelation has a line written to a suffering church: "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life." The same years were hard for Catholics, Baptists, Jews, Muslims and Buddhists under that state too. The Orthodox Church now keeps a feast for its new martyrs, and reads their names.

People are still punished today, in different places and under different powers, for what they believe or how they worship: some Christians, some of other faiths or none. Picture one person in a cell tonight because of what they believe; you don't need their name. If you pray, ask that they be kept faithful and safe; if not, let them be real to you for a while.

945.title: The Christmas truce (1914)
945.hook: soldiers climb out of the trenches to sing carols and share food with the enemy
945.carry: silent night in no man's land
945.howItsDone: At Christmas, churches sing carols such as Silent Night, and some retell the Christmas truce in services that pray for peace between enemies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new martyrs of Russia, and the word martys: a witness, faithful in small hidden ways.

A cold, clear Christmas Eve in Flanders. Two lines of trenches, close enough to shout across. Between them, a strip of mud, wire and shell holes the soldiers call no man's land. Anyone who raises his head above the parapet risks a bullet. Then, on the German side, lights appear: small candles, and in places little Christmas trees set up along the trench. A voice starts singing, and others join. Stille Nacht. Silent night. On the British side, men listen. After a while, someone sings back.

Much of what's known comes from soldiers' letters home. In places along the line, men climbed out of their trenches, unarmed, and walked toward each other. They shook hands and swapped what they had: chocolate, cigarettes, sausage, buttons from their uniforms, addresses to write to after the war. Some letters mention a kick-about with a ball. Both sides used the quiet to bury their dead, and in places they held services together over the graves. Then the truce ended, and the shooting started again. It didn't happen everywhere. In some sections the shooting never stopped. Officers on both sides disapproved, and it was not repeated the same way. So why does it matter? Because of what the soldiers sang. The carols told a story both sides knew: the angels over the shepherds' fields, singing, in the King James Bible, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." Men who had been trying to kill each other found they shared a song, a prayer and a holiday. Jesus once said, "Love your enemies." For a night, in a muddy field, some men did. This week, people kept stepping across something: the color line at Azusa Street, Pandita Ramabai's home for widows, Sundar Singh's water in an Indian cup, Harris the walking prophet, Kimbangu's church from a prison, the martyrs faithful in the camps. And now enemies sharing chocolate between the trenches.

Choose someone you're on the other side of: a rival at work, a relative you argue with. Notice the trench you've both dug, then picture one small thing you could hand across: a compliment you actually mean, a cup of coffee, a question asked out of real curiosity. You don't have to end the war; if you pray, pray for them by name.
Stille Nacht. The German carol German soldiers sang on Christmas Eve 1914, which British troops recognized and answered with their own voices across no man's land.
Your line: silent night in no man's land. For one night, enemies shared a song. A week of crossings, done.

chat.says: Did the Christmas truce really stop the whole war for Christmas?
options: No. In places men met, swapped gifts and buried their dead, but elsewhere the shooting went on.
Yes, the whole Western Front fell quiet, and generals on both sides had agreed to it.
No, it was only a rumor: no soldiers' letters ever mentioned anything like it.
chat.meaning: Soldiers' letters tell of handshakes, gifts and shared burials in places, but it didn't happen everywhere, and the shooting started again.
